payload.name: Count_questions_search_ownership_verbs
payload.description: When a question asks how many of a category a person has or owns as of a time, and generic category+'count' searches miss ownership records, also search with acquisition/possession verbs and discovered instance names.
content: When answering 'how many X does Y have as of [time]', do not stop after searches combining X and 'count'/'number'; ownership evidence often appears in event memories as verbs (adopted, bought, got, received, owns, has).
If initial retrievals lack ownership records, run additional keyword/BM25 searches joining Y with each acquisition/possession verb and the category X (e.g., '[Y] adopted X', '[Y] owns X').
When any retrieved memory names an instance (e.g., a pet name), also search for that instance alongside Y and X to discover co-occurring other instances before finalizing the count.

candidates.solves: The diagnosed cause is that count-of-possessions questions under-recall because memory events use acquisition verbs (adopted, bought) and instance names rather than the category noun plus 'count'. This rule requires verb-based and instance-based supplementary searches when generic category+count searches miss. It applies to any future question enumerating concrete owned or acquired entities (pets, vehicles, children) by a specified person as of a date, not to preference or plan questions.

payload.name: Enumerate purchases with category vocabulary search
payload.description: When a question asks what items someone bought or made for a beneficiary class (pets, children, home, etc.), search using the full set of typical item terms for that class, not just already-retrieved items.
content: Before answering an enumeration question about items bought/created for a beneficiary class (e.g., pets, children, household), identify the class and generate a broad list of concrete category items (for pets: beds, collars, tags, toys, leashes, food, grooming supplies; for children: clothes, toys, books, furniture).
Run at least one additional keyword or hybrid search using these category terms even if prior searches returned memories, and inspect any newly retrieved candidates before finalizing the answer.

candidates.solves: When a question asks to enumerate items a person bought or made for a beneficiary class (e.g., their pets, children, home), retrieval can miss common items because queries are seeded only with items already found. This causes incomplete answers like missing 'dog beds' when searches used 'toys, goodies, jewelry'. The rule is to generate and search the typical category vocabulary of that beneficiary class (e.g., for pets: beds, collars, tags, toys, leashes, food) before concluding, which applies to any future enumeration question about purchases or creations for a group.

payload.name: Expand list answers from implied work mentions
payload.description: Use when a question asks for a list/set of entities (authors, books, people, places) and retrieved memories mention specific works or items that could imply additional list members. Apply before finalizing an answer, after initial retrieval, to expand queries and infer implied entities.
content: When the question asks for a list or set of entities (e.g., authors, books, participants) and initial retrieval returns only one explicit match, do not finalize. Search again using terms derived from the returned memories (titles, names, series) and the target relationship (e.g., author of <title>).

If a memory mentions a well-known work or item (book, movie, product), treat its creator/author/owner as a candidate list member only if other retrieved evidence supports the connection; otherwise keep it as a query expansion.
Repeat search/inspection until additional query variations yield no new supported candidates, then answer with the full set of distinct members supported by visible evidence.

candidates.solves: When a question asks for all members of a set and the first search finds only one explicit match, the agent answers too early. The cause is that memories referencing well-known works (e.g., a book title) imply additional set members (their authors) without containing the query words. The rule uses such mentions as query expansions, infers the implied entity, and continues searching until no new supported candidate appears. This applies to plural list questions, not single-fact questions or entities unsupported by memory.

payload.name: Expand_event_synonyms_before_no_information
payload.description: Use when a question asks how many times an event happened and the first search returns no explicit matches; expand synonym-phrased searches before concluding no information.
content: Before answering 'no information' for an event-count question, run additional keyword or hybrid searches with morphological variants and synonyms of the event term (e.g., rejected → rejection, declined, setback) and related object terms.

Do not treat a single failed keyword search as proof that an event never occurred; expand the query to the subject's associated activities and roles, then re-judge evidence sufficiency before concluding absence.

candidates.solves: Stored events used different wording ('rejection letter', 'setback') than the searched keyword ('rejected'), and the agent stopped after one search. The reusable failure is giving up too early on event-count questions when surface forms differ. Expanding synonyms and related object terms before declaring absence applies to any future count/enumeration question (how many times X happened), not when explicit evidence is already retrieved.

payload.name: Compare entities via per-entity factual searches
payload.description: When a question asks what two or more named entities have in common or what they both share, retrieve factual state/event memories for each entity individually and compare, instead of relying on one abstract similarity query.
content: If the question asks what two or more named entities have in common (e.g., 'what do X and Y both...'), do not rely on a single abstract similarity search. Issue separate searches for each named entity targeting their factual state/event memories (job, career, business, education, residence, major life changes).

After per-entity searches, identify overlapping facts across the entities and answer only from those retrieved memories. If the initial results contain only relationship/support memories without factual states, treat evidence as insufficient and search again for each entity's life-event and state memories.

When a generic semantic query fails to surface factual commonalities, use structured or keyword strategies with each entity's name plus domain predicates (e.g., 'lost job', 'started business', 'owns') to find comparable factual memories.

candidates.solves: Comparative questions such as 'what do X and Y have in common' fail when the agent runs only one abstract similarity query, which surfaces relational/support memories but not each person's factual life events. Diagnosed cause: the query 'common characteristics' missed memories about job loss and starting businesses. Abstract mechanism: generic comparative queries under-retrieve per-entity facts. This rule applies to any future comparison, overlap, or shared-attribute question about named entities, requiring per-entity factual retrieval before answering.

payload.name: List-made-items-retrieval
payload.description: When a question asks to list items a person has made, cooked, or created (e.g., recipes, dishes), apply before answering to run multiple targeted searches that surface specific named items.
content: When the user asks what items a person has made or created, treat it as an enumeration query; do not answer after one generic search.

Run multiple searches: one with the person's name plus action verbs (made, baked, cooked, prepared, created), one with the item category and the person's name, and one for the person's preferences or favorites that may name specific items.

Before answering, verify the retrieved evidence contains specific named items; if not, continue with additional keyword or structured searches using known details (e.g., ingredients, flavors) rather than stopping with generic descriptions.

candidates.solves: When a question asks to enumerate what a person has made or created (e.g., recipes, dishes, projects), a single generic query often misses specific named items stored in event or preference memories. This skill addresses the general failure of retrieval completeness for enumeration questions by requiring multiple targeted searches with action verbs and preference memories, applicable to any future 'what has X made' request.

payload.name: Per-entity expansion for intersection queries
payload.description: Use when a question asks what two or more entities share (e.g., both visited, both like, common plan) and initial retrieval misses evidence or returns only generic memories.
content: If the initial search for a multi-entity intersection query returns no overlap, do not repeat the identical query; issue separate searches for each entity using its name and known aliases.

After each per-entity search, collect concrete attribute values (cities, activities, preferences) from retrieved memories and issue follow-up searches combining each entity with those candidate values.
Conclude 'no information' only after per-entity searches for all entities and candidate-value expansions have been attempted and still yield no supporting memory.

candidates.solves: When a question asks for an intersection or common attribute (e.g., a city both people visited) and the initial hybrid search returns only generic memories for one entity or no overlap, the failure mechanism is searching only the combined query and never issuing per-entity searches with name variants and candidate attribute values. Future equivalent questions benefit by decomposing the query per entity and expanding with concrete values found in retrieved memories before concluding no evidence.

payload.name: Enumerative attribute retrieval with per-category searches
payload.description: Use when a question asks what kinds/types/forms of a thing a person produces, creates, or engages in, and the first search returns generic results.
content: Before answering enumeration questions, split the requested attribute into likely concrete categories (e.g., screenplay/script, book, blog/post, journal, article, poem) and run a separate search for each category, not only the general phrase.
When a memory mentions a specific completed or ongoing artifact of a category, treat it as evidence for that category even if the memory's main topic is another event or experience.
Do not answer an enumeration question after only one top-k search; if additional category searches return no supporting memory, state only the categories with visible evidence.

candidates.solves: When a question asks for all kinds/types of a person's outputs or activities (e.g., writings, creative works, projects), a single top-k hybrid search usually returns only generic or partially matching memories and misses concrete event instances such as completed works, posts, or journals. This skill instructs the agent to enumerate likely categories and run additional targeted searches for each, and to treat concrete event/plan memories mentioning specific formats as evidence, avoiding incomplete answers.

payload.name: Decompose multi-condition retrieval queries
payload.description: When a question asks for an activity or item satisfying two independent conditions (e.g., a person's enjoyment AND benefit to their pet), run separate targeted searches for each condition before combining.
content: When a question requires intersecting two independent facts about a subject (e.g., an activity they enjoy AND a pet they own), run separate retrieval passes: one per condition. Do not rely on a single combined query.
Vary query terms per pass: for enjoyment/hobbies use terms like enjoys, getting into, trying, hobby, activity; for possession/relationship use terms like adopted, has, owns, pet, dog.
Answer only when evidence covers both conditions. If one side is missing, issue additional targeted searches for that condition before finalizing.

candidates.solves: Access failures occur when compound questions require evidence from two independent memory dimensions (e.g., a person's current hobby and their pet ownership) but the agent runs only one combined query that misses one dimension. This skill instructs decomposing such questions into separate sub-queries and verifying evidence for each condition before answering. It applies to any future question asking for an activity or item that must satisfy both a subject preference and a relationship/possession fact, so long as a single memory does not already record the combined activity.

payload.name: Count owned items via acquisition events
payload.description: When asked how many of an item a person has/owns, search for individual acquisition/ownership events before concluding missing information; do not rely on number/count phrasing.
content: If a question asks for a count of items a person owns/has, search for concrete acquisition or ownership events: adopted, bought, received, owns, has a [item], or named instances of the item.
Do not make 'number', 'count', or 'how many' the primary query terms; these often miss individual event memories.
Enumerate distinct named entities/instances from retrieved memories and sum them only when each event clearly indicates a separate item owned by the person.
If retrieval returns only plans, considerations, or other people's items, continue searching with alternative terms before answering 'no information'.

candidates.solves: Diagnosed cause: counting questions fail when retrieval targets the numeric phrasing (e.g., 'how many dogs does X have') and misses individual acquisition/ownership events that establish each owned item. The reusable mechanism applies to any future question asking how many of an item a person has, owns, or has adopted; the count must be assembled from separate event memories, not from a single explicit total. Boundary: not needed when the answer is already stored as an explicit count in one memory.

payload.name: Exhaustive retrieval for counting questions
payload.description: When a question asks how many times or the total number of events a person participated in (e.g., tournaments, competitions), keep searching with varied queries until no new relevant memories are found, then aggregate all distinct events before answering.
content: When the question asks for a count or number of an entity's activities, treat it as an exhaustive count: do not stop after the first top-k search.
Issue additional searches using synonyms and related terms (e.g., 'won', 'participated', 'tournament', 'competition') and increase top-k/depth until the last search returns no new relevant memories.

Before answering, aggregate every distinct event memory that matches the counted activity; verify that the answer equals the total number of distinct events found, not just the first retrieved subset.

candidates.solves: The diagnosed cause is that a count question was answered from a single top-k search, missing several relevant event memories. The reusable mechanism is that numeric questions about an entity's activities require exhaustive retrieval and aggregation, not a first-pass subset. This applies whenever a future question asks for a count or total of an entity's events, across any topic.
